# About this analysis

This script runs Monocle3, a trajectory inference tool that scores consistently high in benchmark papers, on the clustered astrocyte Seurat object. I use the clustered object because the untrustworthy clusters have already been removed there. The Seurat object is converted to a `cell_data_set`, a trajectory graph is learned on the astrocyte UMAP, and pseudotime is calculated from a chosen root. Afterwards I run additional Monocle3 tests (`graph_test()`, gene modules, pseudotime per condition) to find genes that change along the trajectory.

### theme_quarto() and theme_manuscript()

I created my own themes to add to figures. `theme_quarto()` is used to add themes to figures as displayed in the Quarto document and saved to disk as `.pdf` or `.png`. `theme_manuscript()` is used to add themes to figures as they will end up in the manuscript. I can already add arguments with `theme()` or specific themes (e.g. `theme_classic()`, my personal favourite) to plots; adding `theme()` afterwards keeps whatever was added in `theme()` before it, unless I specify that arugment here - that's why I allowed to specify some things within my functions as well.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-06-helper-themes
theme_quarto <- function(
    legend_position = "right", 
    plot_title = element_blank()
    ) {
    theme(
      plot.title = plot_title,
      legend.position = legend_position
    )
}

theme_manuscript <- function(
    legend_position = "none",
    plot_title = element_blank(),
    axis_title_size = 8,
    axis_text_size = 6
    ) {
    theme(
      plot.title = plot_title,
      legend.position = legend_position,
      axis.title = element_text(size = axis_title_size),
      axis.text = element_text(size = axis_text_size),
      legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm"), 
      legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
      legend.title = element_text(size = 9)
    )
}

```

### save_plot()

This document displays all the figures I make, but I also want them saved to disk — both as `.png` and `.pdf`. I only need to provide the ggplot object, a filename (without extension), and optionally the width and height of the figure and additional arguments put into themes.

The figures for my written report contain subfigures spread across multiple scripts. Since I want to assemble these panel figures via R code rather than by hand, `save_plot()` can also optionally save the plot object itself to disk as an .rds file, for a final script to later combine with `patchwork`. Set figure to the name the figure should carry in the report (e.g. `"SF1A"`) to trigger this; leave it `NULL` (the default) to just save the `.png`/`.pdf` as normal.

A live ggplot object carries its underlying data along with it — for plots built from large Seurat objects, this can balloon the saved file to gigabytes. To avoid this, `save_plot()` converts the object to a grob (a static, pre-rendered drawing, with no data attached) before saving it as `.rds`. This is controlled by the `grob` argument, and defaults to `TRUE`, since converting a small plot costs nothing but forgetting to convert a large one is expensive. Set `grob = FALSE` only if a later step specifically needs the original, live ggplot object rather than its rendered form.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-05-helper-save-plot
save_plot <- function(
    p, filename, 
    width = 10, height = 6, 
    figure = NULL, grob = TRUE, apply_theme = TRUE, 
    add_tag = TRUE, tag_text_size = 14,
    legend_pos_manuscript = "none"
    ) {
  ## Save image on disk as png and pdf
  # Add Quarto-specific theme, unless the plot has its own custom theme
  if (apply_theme) {
    p_image <- p + theme_quarto()
  } else {
    p_image <- p
  }
  file_png <- file.path(dir_fig, paste0(filename, ".png"))
  ggsave(file_png, p_image, width = width, height = height, dpi = 150)
  file_pdf <- file.path(dir_fig, paste0(filename, ".pdf"))
  ggsave(file_pdf, p_image, width = width, height = height, dpi = 150)
  
  ## Save the ggplot object on disk as an rds file 
  if (!is.null(figure)) {
    # Add tag if needed
    if (add_tag) {
      tag <- str_extract(figure, "[A-Z]$")
      p <- p + 
        labs(tag = tag) + 
        theme(
          plot.tag = element_text(
            face = "bold", 
            size = tag_text_size, 
            hjust = 0, vjust = 0
            )
        )
    }
    # Add manuscript-specific theme, unless the plot has its own custom theme
    if (apply_theme) {
      p <- p + theme_manuscript(legend_pos_manuscript)
    }
    file_rds <- file.path(dir_man, paste0(figure, ".rds"))
    # Convert the object to a grob if needed
    if (grob) {
      p <- ggplotGrob(p)
    }
    # Save on disk
    saveRDS(p, file_rds)
  }
}
```

### print_tabset()

Quarto cannot cross-reference figures that are made inside a loop. To still display the plots of a loop in this document, I collect them in a named list and show them as tabs with `print_tabset()`. The names of the list become the tab titles. It also accepts data frames (shown as a table). This function writes raw Quarto markdown, so the chunk that calls it needs the chunk option `#| output: asis`. `heading_level` should be one deeper than the heading above the chunk.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-07-helper-print-tabset
print_tabset <- function(obj_list, heading_level = 3) {
  cat("::: {.panel-tabset}\n\n")
  for (nm in names(obj_list)) {
    cat(strrep("#", heading_level), " ", nm, "\n\n", sep = "")
    obj <- obj_list[[nm]]
    if (inherits(obj, "ggplot")) {
      print(obj)
    } else if (is.data.frame(obj)) {
      cat(knitr::kable(obj, format = "pipe"), sep = "\n")
    }
    cat("\n\n")
  }
  cat(":::\n\n")
}
```

# Convert the Seurat object to a cell_data_set

```{r}

```

Next, I convert the object to a `cell_data_set`. I made dimensionality reductions specifically for the astrocyte subset, so I check whether my astrocyte UMAP has been transferred correctly. `learn_graph()` cannot take a specific reduction as an argument, and only grabs `"UMAP"` by default. A simple solution is to copy the coordinates of the astrocyte UMAP into `"UMAP"`.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-09-convert-to-cds
cds <- as.cell_data_set(seu)

# Check which reduced dimensions have been transferred
reducedDims(cds)

# Overwrite the default "UMAP" with the astrocyte UMAP
reducedDim(cds, "UMAP") <- reducedDim(cds, reduction_cds)

# [ADD] Verify the copy with a one-line check (e.g. identical() or all.equal()
# on the two matrices). Why is it better to *test* this than to trust that the
# line above worked?
```

# Partitions and clusters

Monocle3 trajectory inference does not require clustering, but it does need *partitions*, which are found with `cluster_cells()`. In short, each partition becomes a separate trajectory. When I used the pre-QC astrocytes (including mixed-lineage cells), `cluster_cells()` separated the mixed-lineage cells from the 'pure' astrocytes. I assume that with the post-QC astrocytes it will find a single partition.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-10-cluster-cells
cds <- cluster_cells(cds)

# Check whether there is indeed only one partition
table(partitions(cds))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-02-partitions
#| fig-cap: "Monocle3 partitions on the astrocyte UMAP."
p_partitions <- plot_cells(
  cds,
  color_cells_by = "partition",
  show_trajectory_graph = FALSE # Otherwise it displays a previous graph
)
p_partitions
```

```{r}
#| label: chunk-11-save-partitions
#| echo: false
save_plot(p_partitions, "monocle3_plot_partitions")
```

Just out of curiosity, I also plot the Monocle3 clusters, to see whether they agree with the Seurat clusters.

```{r}
#| label: fig-03-clusters
#| fig-cap: "Monocle3 clusters on the astrocyte UMAP."
p_clusters <- plot_cells(
  cds,
  color_cells_by = "cluster",
  show_trajectory_graph = FALSE
)
p_clusters
```

```{r}
#| label: chunk-12-save-clusters
#| echo: false
save_plot(p_clusters, "monocle3_plot_cluster")
```

# Learning the trajectory graph

A single line of code infers the trajectory.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-13-learn-graph
cds <- learn_graph(cds)
```

I colour by `col`, defined at the top, so I can easily change it later (for example, if I make an annotation column in Seurat and want to use that here). The first plot shows the trajectory and where it branches.

```{r}
#| label: fig-04-trajectory
#| fig-cap: "Monocle3 trajectory on the astrocyte UMAP, with leaves and branch points labelled."
p_trajectory <- plot_cells(
  cds,
  color_cells_by = col,
  label_cell_groups = FALSE,
  label_leaves = TRUE,
  label_branch_points = TRUE,
  graph_label_size = 2
)
p_trajectory
```

```{r}
#| label: chunk-14-save-trajectory
#| echo: false
save_plot(p_trajectory, paste0("monocle3_traj_", col))
```

The second plot also shows the principal points. I use these to select where pseudotime should start.

```{r}
#| label: fig-05-principal-points
#| fig-cap: "Monocle3 trajectory with principal points labelled, used to select the pseudotime root."
p_principal_points <- plot_cells(
  cds,
  color_cells_by = col,
  label_cell_groups = FALSE,
  label_leaves = TRUE,
  label_branch_points = TRUE,
  graph_label_size = 2,
  label_principal_points = TRUE # Needed to choose the root
)
p_principal_points
```

```{r}
#| label: chunk-15-save-principal-points
#| echo: false
save_plot(p_principal_points, paste0("monocle3_pp_", col))
```

I save the `cds` object on disk, so I can examine later which principal points are interesting.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-16-save-cds
saveRDS(cds, file.path(dir_data, "seu_shortread_monocle3_cds.rds"))
```

# Pseudotime

## Pseudotime for every principal point

To decide where pseudotime should start, I make a figure for every principal point and collect them in a single PDF (instead of one `.png` per principal point). This is certainly not the most elegant approach, but it works for now. The plots in this PDF are not displayed in the HTML output.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-17-pseudotime-all-roots
principal_point_names <- colnames(cds@principal_graph_aux[["UMAP"]]$dp_mst)

pdf(file = file.path(dir_fig, "monocle3_pseudotime.pdf"))
for (pp in principal_point_names) {
  # [CHANGED] In the .R script, `cds` was overwritten in every iteration, so
  # after the loop `cds` held the pseudotime of the *last* root. Now I use a
  # temporary object so `cds` stays untouched.
  cds_tmp <- order_cells(cds, root_pr_nodes = pp)

  p <- plot_cells(
    cds_tmp,
    color_cells_by = "pseudotime",
    label_cell_groups = FALSE,
    label_leaves = TRUE,
    label_branch_points = TRUE,
    graph_label_size = 2
  ) +
    labs(title = paste0("Pseudotime for root ", pp))
  print(p) # print() is needed inside a loop
}
dev.off()
```

## Pseudotime from the chosen root

After inspecting the principal points and the PDF, I pick one root (`root_node`, defined at the top) and calculate pseudotime from it.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-18-order-cells
cds <- order_cells(cds, root_pr_nodes = root_node)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-06-pseudotime
#| fig-cap: "Monocle3 pseudotime from the chosen root principal point."
# [CHECK] theme_quarto() removes the legend, but for pseudotime the colour
# scale *is* the information. Same question as in fig-01.
p_pseudotime <- plot_cells(
  cds,
  color_cells_by = "pseudotime",
  label_cell_groups = FALSE,
  label_leaves = TRUE,
  label_branch_points = TRUE,
  graph_label_size = 2
)
p_pseudotime
```

```{r}
#| label: chunk-19-save-pseudotime
#| echo: false
save_plot(p_pseudotime, "monocle3_pseudotime_root")
```

# Additional tests: genes that change along the trajectory

<!-- [ADD] FIRST ATTEMPT, UNTESTED. This whole section is new code. Run it
chunk by chunk, read the error messages and fix them yourself. Likely failure
points are marked with [CHECK]. -->

Monocle3 offers `graph_test()` (note: not `test_graph()`), which uses Moran's *I* to test whether a gene's expression is spatially autocorrelated on the trajectory graph. A high Moran's *I* means that cells close to each other on the trajectory have similar expression, so the gene varies along the trajectory.

## Preparing the cds for testing

A `cell_data_set` made from a Seurat object may lack size factors, and `graph_test()` needs them. I also restrict the test to genes expressed in at least `min_expr_fraction` of cells, to reduce runtime and the multiple-testing burden.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-20-prepare-tests
# [CHECK] as.cell_data_set() should set gene_short_name; if not, add it
if (!"gene_short_name" %in% colnames(rowData(cds))) {
  rowData(cds)$gene_short_name <- rownames(cds)
}

# [CHECK] Does the cds contain raw counts? Look at counts(cds)[1:5, 1:5]
cds <- estimate_size_factors(cds)

# Fraction of cells expressing each gene
expr_fraction <- Matrix::rowMeans(counts(cds) > 0)
genes_test <- names(expr_fraction)[expr_fraction >= min_expr_fraction]
length(genes_test)
```

## graph_test()

```{r}
#| label: chunk-21-graph-test
# [CHECK] This can take long. Run it as a SLURM job with multiple cores rather
# than in RStudio. neighbor_graph = "principal_graph" tests variation along the
# trajectory; "knn" would test variation between neighbouring cells instead.
graph_test_res <- graph_test(
  cds[genes_test, ],
  neighbor_graph = "principal_graph",
  cores = n_cores
)

graph_test_res <- graph_test_res %>%
  rownames_to_column("gene") %>%
  arrange(q_value, desc(morans_I))

# Use write_csv2, as my Microsoft Office with Dutch settings prefers ";" as sep
write_csv2(graph_test_res, file.path(dir_tab, "graph_test_results.csv"))
```

```{r}
#| label: chunk-22-graph-test-significant
# [CHANGE] Look at the distribution of morans_I before trusting morans_cutoff:
# summary(graph_test_res$morans_I)
genes_sig <- graph_test_res %>%
  filter(q_value < q_cutoff, morans_I > morans_cutoff) %>%
  pull(gene)

length(genes_sig)
kable(head(graph_test_res, 10))
```

The top genes (by Moran's *I*) are plotted on the trajectory.

```{r}
#| label: fig-07-top-genes
#| fig-cap: "Expression of the top 6 genes by Moran's I along the Monocle3 trajectory."
genes_top <- graph_test_res %>%
  filter(q_value < q_cutoff) %>%
  slice_max(morans_I, n = 6) %>%
  pull(gene)

p_top_genes <- plot_cells(
  cds,
  genes = genes_top,
  show_trajectory_graph = FALSE,
  label_cell_groups = FALSE
)
p_top_genes
```

```{r}
#| label: chunk-23-save-top-genes
#| echo: false
save_plot(p_top_genes, "monocle3_top_genes", width = 12, height = 8)
```

## Gene modules

I group the significant genes into modules of genes with similar behaviour along the trajectory.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-24-gene-modules
# [CHECK] find_gene_modules() needs gene loadings from preprocess_cds(), which
# is not present in a cds converted from Seurat. I run it on a *copy*, so the
# PCA stored in `cds` (transferred from Seurat) is not overwritten.
cds_modules <- preprocess_cds(cds[genes_sig, ], num_dim = 50)

# [CHANGE] resolution is arbitrary here; try a few values and compare.
gene_module_df <- find_gene_modules(cds_modules, resolution = 1e-2,
                                    cores = n_cores)

write_csv2(gene_module_df, file.path(dir_tab, "monocle3_gene_modules.csv"))
table(gene_module_df$module)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-08-gene-modules
#| fig-cap: "Aggregated expression of each Monocle3 gene module on the astrocyte UMAP."
p_gene_modules <- plot_cells(
  cds,
  genes = gene_module_df,
  show_trajectory_graph = FALSE,
  label_cell_groups = FALSE
)
p_gene_modules
```

```{r}
#| label: chunk-25-save-gene-modules
#| echo: false
save_plot(p_gene_modules, "monocle3_gene_modules", width = 12, height = 8)
```
